High‑sensitivity screening models using large language models (LLMs) consistently achieve sensitivities at or above 90% in several diagnostic accuracy studies. Li et al. reported overall abstract‑screening sensitivity of 90% (range 90–97%) across two datasets, with specificity varying from 59% to 93% [R0011]. Qiu et al. demonstrated 98% to 100% sensitivity for abstract screening across three independent datasets, with specificity between 80.6% and 93% [R0079]. The Review Copilot system achieved 99.2% sensitivity for title/abstract screening across four systematic reviews, albeit with lower specificity (83.6%) [R0049]. In contrast, studies using alternative LLMs reported more modest sensitivities: Oami et al. observed a modified‑prompt sensitivity of 0.91 after optimisation, while the original prompt yielded 0.75 [R0010]; Ramchandani et al. found peri‑operative recall of 0.89 but pre‑operative recall of 0.67 [R0014]; López‑Pineda et al. reported 77.5% sensitivity for Llama 3 and 56.2% for ChatGPT‑4o mini [R0037]; and Yamoah et al. achieved 88% sensitivity with a dual‑reviewer reference standard on a large sample of 15,307 abstracts [R0073]. Additional evidence from benchmark testing showed ChatGPT v4.0 reaching 93% sensitivity on the Bannach‑Brown database [R0035], and a fine‑tuned 1.2 B‑parameter model attaining 91.18% sensitivity on 8,277 records [R0096]. Across studies, higher sensitivities are associated with prompt optimisation, larger LLM versions (e.g., GPT‑4), and thorough dual‑reviewer reference standards, though specificity often declines when sensitivity is maximised.

DISCUSSION:
The 21 diagnostic accuracy studies show that large language models (LLMs) can achieve high sensitivity for title and abstract screening, often exceeding 90% when prompt optimisation, ensemble methods, or fine‑tuning are applied. High‑sensitivity models such as those reported by Li et al. and Qiu et al. reached 90–100% sensitivity, though specificity varied widely (59–93%) [R0011,R0079,R0049]. Ensemble and prompt‑optimisation strategies consistently improved performance, with chain‑of‑thought or zero‑shot prompting raising recall while maintaining or improving precision [R0010,R0025,R0028,R0061,R0138,R0103,R0145]. Fine‑tuned, domain‑specific LLMs demonstrated superior balanced accuracy compared with general‑purpose models, achieving sensitivities around 81–91% and specificities up to 96% [R0069,R0096,R0072,R0045,R0058,R0085]. A prospective study reported pooled sensitivity of 0.73 and specificity of 0.99, which improved to 0.98 sensitivity after prompt revision, suggesting that engineering choices markedly affect outcomes [R0018]. Across themes, the evidence is moderate in certainty due to observational designs, some risk of bias, and heterogeneity in reference standards.
Most studies were observational diagnostic accuracy designs with some concerns for bias, such as unblinded reference standards, single‑reviewer coding, or potential overlap between training data and test sets, which may inflate performance estimates [R0018,R0011,R0079]. Reference standards varied (dual‑reviewer, single‑reviewer, or consensus), limiting comparability. Sample sizes and reporting of confidence intervals were inconsistent, reducing precision for some estimates. The heterogeneity of LLM versions, prompting strategies, and datasets introduces indirectness, and few studies evaluated full‑text screening or real‑world workflow integration, restricting generalisability.
Practitioners should view LLMs as promising tools that can achieve high sensitivity in title/abstract screening when carefully optimised, but they should not replace human reviewers without validation in the specific review context. Future research should employ blinded, multi‑reviewer reference standards, report detailed performance metrics, and assess LLMs across diverse topics and full‑text screening stages. Comparative studies of fine‑tuned versus zero‑shot models, and investigations of ensemble approaches in real‑time systematic review workflows, will help clarify the conditions under which LLMs can reliably augment or replace manual screening.

ABSTRACT:


**Background:** Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for title and abstract screening in systematic reviews, yet their diagnostic accuracy compared with human reviewers remains unclear.

**Objectives:** To identify and summarise primary research evaluating LLM performance for title/abstract screening, to compare LLM accuracy with human reviewers using standard measures (sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1), and to assess methodological quality and factors influencing performance.

**Methods:** We searched PubMed, Europe PMC, arXiv and Semantic Scholar on 2026-11-11. Of 239 records identified, 50 were screened on title and abstract by two independent AI reviewers with adjudication of disagreements, 33 reports were assessed for eligibility and 21 studies were included. Data were extracted with supporting quotations that were verified automatically against the source, risk of bias was appraised with design-specific tools, and findings were synthesised narratively by theme.

**Results:** Across 21 diagnostic‑accuracy studies (risk of bias: 20 some concerns, 1 unclear), high‑sensitivity models reported sensitivities of 90%–100% but specificities varied from 59% to 93% (e.g., Li et al. 90% sensitivity, Qiu et al. 98%–100%). Ensemble and prompt‑optimisation approaches improved performance, raising sensitivity to up to 100% while maintaining precision (e.g., Oami et al. sensitivity 0.91, specificity 0.98). Fine‑tuned, domain‑specific LLMs achieved balanced accuracy up to 93.3% with higher specificity than general‑purpose models. A prospective study reported pooled sensitivity 0.73 (95% CI 0.57‑0.85) and specificity 0.99 (95% CI 0.97‑0.99), improving to 0.98 sensitivity after prompt revision. Certainty of evidence was rated moderate for each theme due to observational designs, risk of bias, and heterogeneity.

**Conclusions:** LLMs show potential to identify relevant records, with some models meeting a 90% sensitivity threshold, but performance is variable and the certainty of evidence is moderate to low. Prompt optimisation, ensemble methods, and fine‑tuning appear to enhance accuracy, while variability in reference standards and bias limit confidence in generalising findings.

response: Automated title‑and‑abstract screening is widely promoted as a way to lessen the labour‑intensive workload of systematic reviews, yet the empirical evidence for large language models (LLMs) in this role remains fragmented. Several recent investigations have begun to evaluate LLMs for screening, reporting mixed accuracy and highlighting the need for systematic synthesis of comparative performance data [R0108]. Early work has demonstrated that fine‑tuned, smaller LLMs can be promising for large‑scale reviews, but these studies have been limited to single models or specific domains [R0096]. More comprehensive assessments have emerged, testing state‑of‑the‑art models such as GPT‑4 and GPT‑4o Mini against human reviewers and reporting sensitivity, specificity, and workload reductions across thousands of records and multiple clinical topics [R0045, R0028, R0072]. Nonetheless, direct head‑to‑head comparisons between LLMs and traditional supervised machine‑learning baselines are scarce, and the methodological quality of existing reports varies, making it difficult for reviewers to gauge reliability and to decide whether to adopt LLMs in practice [R0058]. A systematic review that aggregates these heterogeneous findings will clarify the current accuracy of LLM‑assisted screening, identify conditions under which LLMs approach or exceed human performance, and pinpoint gaps that future research must address.

High‑sensitivity screening models using large language models (LLMs) consistently report sensitivities at or above 90% for title and abstract screening. Nordmann et al. achieved 88%–89% sensitivity on 15,307 abstracts with a dual‑reviewer reference standard, illustrating that even large samples can yield sub‑90% sensitivity when the LLM or workflow differs [R0073]. Across studies, higher sensitivities are associated with larger LLMs (GPT‑4 variants), refined prompts, and fine‑tuning, whereas variability stems from differing reference standards, sample sizes, and reporting completeness.

DISCUSSION:
Across 21 diagnostic accuracy studies, large language models (LLMs) generally achieved high sensitivity for title and abstract screening, often exceeding 90% when using the most advanced models (e.g., GPT‑4 variants) and optimized prompts [R0011,R0010,R0079,R0049]. Sensitivity tended to be lower for earlier or smaller models such as Llama 3 and ChatGPT‑4o mini, highlighting the influence of model version and prompting [R0037,R0073]. Ensemble and prompt‑optimization approaches consistently boosted performance, raising sensitivity to 0.91–1.00 while maintaining specificity above 0.95 in several large datasets, though precision sometimes declined with extreme class imbalance [R0010,R0025,R0028,R0061,R0138]. Fine‑tuned, domain‑specific LLMs outperformed general‑purpose counterparts, achieving accuracies around 93%, sensitivities of 81–91% and specificities up to 96% [R0069,R0096,R0072]. A single prospective study reported pooled sensitivity of 0.73 and specificity of 0.99, with post‑hoc prompt revisions improving sensitivity to 0.98, suggesting that prompt engineering can markedly affect outcomes [R0018]. Overall, the evidence is of moderate certainty due to some concerns about bias, inconsistency across models and reference standards, and occasional incomplete reporting.
Most studies were observational diagnostic accuracy designs with some concerns for bias, including lack of blinding, unclear handling of confounding, and potential overlap between LLM training data and screened systematic reviews [R0018,R0037,R0073]. Sample sizes and reporting completeness varied widely, limiting the precision of pooled estimates. Heterogeneity in reference standards (single versus dual reviewer, consensus versus adjudication) and in prompt or fine‑tuning procedures contributed to inconsistency across findings. Few studies evaluated full‑text screening, and many relied on retrospective datasets, reducing external validity.
The findings suggest that LLMs, particularly when fine‑tuned or used within ensemble and prompt‑optimized workflows, can reliably support title and abstract screening, potentially reducing reviewer workload while maintaining high sensitivity. Practitioners should adopt rigorous prompt engineering and consider ensemble strategies to balance sensitivity and precision. Future research should conduct prospective, blinded comparisons, standardize reference standards, and explore the impact of training‑data overlap. Reporting of sample characteristics, blinding procedures, and detailed performance metrics will be essential to strengthen the evidence base.

ABSTRACT:


**Background:** Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to automate title and abstract screening in systematic reviews, yet their diagnostic accuracy relative to human reviewers remains unclear.

**Objectives:** To identify and summarise primary research evaluating LLM performance for title and abstract screening, to compare LLM accuracy with that of human reviewers using standard measures (sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1), and to assess methodological quality and factors influencing performance.

**Methods:** We searched PubMed, Europe PMC, arXiv and Semantic Scholar on 2026-11-11. Of 239 records identified, 50 were screened on title and abstract by two independent AI reviewers with adjudication of disagreements, 33 reports were assessed for eligibility and 21 studies were included. Data were extracted with supporting quotations that were verified automatically against the source, risk of bias was appraised with design-specific tools, and findings were synthesised narratively by theme.

**Results:** Across 21 diagnostic‑accuracy studies, high‑sensitivity models (e.g., GPT‑4 variants) reported sensitivities ≥90% (e.g., 90% across 3,715 abstracts, 0.91 sensitivity on 16,669 records, 98–100% on three datasets) with specificity ranging 59%–93%. Ensemble and prompt‑optimization approaches raised sensitivity to 0.91–1.00 while maintaining specificity >0.95, though precision fell with extreme class imbalance. Fine‑tuned, domain‑specific LLMs achieved accuracies up to 93.3%, sensitivities 81–91% and specificities up to 96%. A prospective study reported pooled sensitivity 0.73 (95% CI 0.57‑0.85) and specificity 0.99 (95% CI 0.97‑0.99), improving to 0.98 sensitivity after prompt revision. Risk‑of‑bias was rated ‘some concerns’ for 20 studies and ‘unclear’ for one; no study was low or high risk.

**Conclusions:** LLMs demonstrate moderate‑to‑high sensitivity for title and abstract screening, often matching or exceeding human reviewers, especially when using advanced models, prompt engineering, or ensemble methods. Specificity is variable, and precision can decline with class imbalance. Evidence certainty is moderate due to some concerns about bias and inconsistency across models, prompts and reference standards.
